title: Analysing Misinformation Sharing Amongst College Students in India During COVID-19
screen_reason: Online questionnaire of 359 Indian college students (30 Oct - 10 Nov 2020). Table 1 gives full frequency distributions for two in-scope self-report items: the perceived extent to which friends share misinformation (62.4% say at least 'very few people' do) and the respondent's own misinformation sharing (19.5% share at least sometimes; 80.5% never). Both are shares of survey respondents with a stated denominator, so RECALL rows qualify. Future-sharing intention is excluded as hypothetical.

estimates.country: India (data collected in parts of Rajasthan and Maharashtra states)
estimates.platform: Social media generally (no platform named in the item; survey circulated by email and WhatsApp)
estimates.measure_type: % of college students who report that at least a few of their friends share misinformation on social media
estimates.value_raw: n = 224, 62.4% (Table 1: very few people 150 / 41.80%, many people 60 / 16.70%, everyone 14 / 3.90%; no one 135 / 37.60%)
estimates.denominator: 359 valid respondents (of 360 received): college students in parts of Rajasthan and Maharashtra, India, reached through a snowball-circulated Google Form; 79.4% male, mean age 21.0, 74.4% undergraduate
estimates.definition: Answered 'very few people', 'many people' or 'everyone' (rather than 'no one') to 'How many of your friends share misinformation on social media?' on a 4-point scale
estimates.misinfo_def: "Misinformation is 'false information that is spread, regardless of any intent to mislead.'"; also "Misinformation is defined as information that has been shown to be inaccurate". The definition was shown to respondents in the questionnaire.
estimates.source_quote: A majority of respondents (n=224, 62.4%) reported that their friends have shared misinformation sometimes on social media platforms (Table 1); the mean was 1.87 (SD = 0.82) on a 4-point scale (with 1 implying ”nobody” and 4 implying ”everybody”).
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.1 'Perceptions on misinformation sharing', p. 675; Table 1 question 1
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondent's own perception; the questionnaire supplied a definition of misinformation and some illustrative scenarios, but no external verification of any item. Non-probability snowball sample.
estimates.moderator_quote: The data analysed for this study is new and collected from parts of Rajasthan and Maharashtra states of India using a snowball sampling technique with a well-designed questionnaire.
estimates.notes: This is the 'perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment' form of recall, which the protocol admits: the respondent reports how much misinformation circulates among their friends, not their own encounters, so recall_subtype = exposure is a judgement rather than a literal 'did you see it' item. 62.4% is verbatim and reconciles exactly with the Table 1 frequencies (150+60+14 = 224 of 359). It is roughly three times the self-reported own-sharing figure (19.5%), which the authors read as social-desirability bias in self-reports. Quote fixed to the exact characters of the text (the previous version used straight quotation marks where the PDF prints typographic ones).

estimates.notes: FLAGGED FOR ADJUDICATION. The value is verbatim and is a share of the same 359 respondents, so R8 permits keeping it, and it is a looser ('might be wrong') variant of the 19.5% item - hence definition_variant = true. But it cannot be traced to any tabulated question, and it does not reconcile with the paper's own MSI variable 1 ('Do you think the information that you spread is misinformation? No-0 / Yes-1'), whose 'Yes' branch implies 41.4% (21.8% + 19.6% from Figure 6). The paper is internally inconsistent in several places (see missed_or_uncertain), so this row should probably be dropped if the review needs one estimate per construct per study; if kept, it should never be pooled alongside the 19.5% row, which measures the same respondents. Quote trimmed to the contiguous verbatim span; a running page header ('680 Priyanka Harjule et al. / Procedia Computer Science 218 (2023) 671-685') is glued into the middle of this sentence in the .txt rendering, so the clause 'that the information they shared over social media might be wrong information' cannot be quoted contiguously with the value.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Future sharing intention (Table 1 question 3: 75.77% 'surely will not share', so 24.2% allow they might or will) is explicitly excluded by the protocol as a hypothetical sharing intention. (2) The Misinformation Sharing Index distribution (Figure 6: no sharing 58.7%, sometimes sharing 21.8%, actively sharing 19.6%) would give 41.4% sharing at least sometimes, but that is a CROSS-CATEGORY SUM, which R8 forbids; and 58.7% is the complement, also forbidden. No MSI row was therefore made, even though the MSI is the paper's headline construct. (3) The abstract in this text file is OCR-damaged at the key number ('Results reveal that about 62.4friends somehow share misinformation'), so the 62.4% row rests on the body text and Table 1, which are clean and mutually consistent. (4) INTERNAL CONTRADICTIONS an adjudicator should see: the Discussion claims 'about 80.3% of males actively share misinformation on the social media platforms', but Table 4's 81.7% is the share of the ALWAYS-SHARING group who are male, not the share of males who always share - the authors misread their own table, and I did not extract it. Similarly 'males 35.0%, females 18.0%' for undergraduate sharing has no denominator anywhere in the text. (5) Subgroup means by gender and education (Figures 4 and 5) are scale means on 4-point items, not shares. (6) Consequence and feedback items (74.7% bad societal consequences; 66.4% anxiety and trust issues; 48.4% sometimes get feedback) are about perceived effects and post-hoc correction, not exposure or sharing prevalence. (7) Motivation items (Table 5, Table A.6) are 5-point means. (8) The literature-review figure 'almost 60% of total respondents never actually verified the source of information they received' is quoted from Kim & Sin and excluded by R8. (9) TOPIC JUDGEMENT CALL: coded general_news because the Table 1 items ask about 'misinformation' with no topic restriction; the study's framing, title and several other items are COVID-19-specific, so an adjudicator may prefer topic = covid19.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey. Google Forms questionnaire (55 questions across socio-demography, perception, motivations, information characteristics, possible consequences, post-pandemic effects) circulated by email and WhatsApp to college students in parts of Rajasthan and Maharashtra, India, with respondents encouraged to forward it - explicit snowball, non-probability sampling. Fielded 30 October 2020 07:00 IST to 10 November 2020 17:00 IST; 360 responses received, 359 valid after individual checking. Informed consent collected on entry. English-language and internet access required. Sample is heavily skewed: 79.4% male, mean age 21.0, 74.4% undergraduate, 64.1% urban, all social media users. No weighting and no response rate (open link). All misinformation measures are single-item self-reports on 4-point scales with a definition supplied in the questionnaire; no external verification, no test-retest, no reliability statistics for the scales, and the misinformation sharing index (MSI) is an unvalidated 2-item sum scored 0/1/11. Analysis: descriptive statistics, independent-sample t-tests, chi-square, correlation matrix; PCA and LDA were attempted and abandoned. Authors' own stated limitations: self-reported behaviour on a socially undesirable act, non-probability sampling, and small sample, so 'it can not represent all college students in India'.
